At this stage, the dry mass of the neonates is exceptionally low, recorded at 0.000014 grams , while the corresponding wet weight is 0.00004 grams [Wwb = 0.00004 grams]. The brief embryonic development and the period spent within the marsupium are highly temperature-dependent; under laboratory conditions maintained at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the time from oviposition to release from the brood pouch is approximately 11.3 days [ab = approximately 11.3 days], representing the age at birth. This rapid early development is characteristic of a species adapted to variable temperate and subtropical habitats, where a relatively short generation time facilitates population persistence. The juvenile amphipods immediately begin grazing on epiphytic algae and detritus, initiating the exogenous feeding phase that will support a period of substantial somatic growth before the attainment of sexual maturity.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, they undergo a series of molting events that drive a pronounced allometric shift in body proportions. Sexual dimorphism becomes increasingly apparent as the amphipods approach their asymptotic size, with males generally attaining larger body dimensions than females in this species. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum body size achieved under resource-rich conditions, is 0.915 centimeters [Li = 0.915 centimeters]. However, this asymptotic size is rarely reached in nature due to predation and seasonal resource limitation. When food is abundant, the maximum total female length recorded is 0.56 centimeters , whereas males can grow considerably larger, reaching a maximum total male length of 0.78 centimeters . This disparity in size between the sexes has implications for reproductive behavior, as larger males often have an advantage in contests for access to gravid females. The ultimate dry weight of an adult of either sex is approximately 0.0034354 grams , and the corresponding ultimate wet weight reaches 0.0174941 grams [Wwi = 0.0174941 grams], representing the peak body condition an individual can sustain.

This elevated reproductive output is a critical life-history trait that allows populations to recover quickly from disturbances or to exploit ephemeral resources. In contrast, the species exhibits a remarkably long potential lifespan when maintained at cooler temperatures, reflecting the metabolic constraints imposed by lower thermal regimes. For instance, the maximum recorded life span at the mean annual temperature of Marion Lake, which is approximately 10 °C [T = 10 °C], is 480.0 days [am = 480.0 days]. This extended longevity at low temperatures is a classic expression of the temperature-size rule and has been documented in several populations of this species.

The ecological success of Hyalella azteca across a wide latitudinal range can be attributed to its remarkable thermal plasticity and flexible life-history tactics. This amphipod serves as a crucial trophic link in freshwater food webs, converting periphyton and detrital matter into high-quality animal biomass consumed by fish, waterfowl, and predatory invertebrates. Comparative studies with congeneric species, such as Hyalella montezuma, reveal that Hyalella azteca possesses a relatively smaller body size but a higher intrinsic rate of population increase, a strategy suited to more variable and less stable lacustrine and lotic environments. Future work on the physiological mechanisms underlying its metabolic compensation across temperatures, particularly concerning the enzymatic kinetics of cellular respiration, will further illuminate the evolutionary trade-offs that define its niche.
